paragraphs: Decision center: whether, with prescription specifications, model and impression quality, material and process parameters, occlusion and seating precision and delivery deadlines all applying at the same time, one can turn impression work and modeling, wax patterns and casting, porcelain build-up and polishing, and inspection and delivery into a genuine, traceable processing loop that meets quality requirements; the focus is not on “looking right” but on making every restoration meet the agreed functional and appearance requirements when the dentist seats it.

Worth trying first: willing to do fine manual work for long periods, able to accept repeated polishing and repeated verification, willing to follow the work order and process specifications without changing the prescription on one's own, interested in hand feel, spatial sense, color discrimination and dimensional precision, and able to record anomalies, rework and process parameters faithfully.

Needs caution: if it is hard to keep hands steady and stay focused for long periods, if one is sensitive to material irritants such as gypsum dust and resin or metal odors, if one is unwilling to repeatedly verify dimensions and colors, if one prefers quick results and does not accept rework, or if one tends to modify the specifications set by the dentist by feel, the actual work will not match expectations.

Low-risk verification: complete the paper exercise for the entry case D-01 covering deviation in three dimensions, missing work-order items and version conflicts, then compare it with the reference delivery and the seven-day plan; no real impressions or equipment are used, and it only observes preferences for verification, documentation and rework feedback, and does not equal training completion or hiring.
Decision center: whether one can turn prescription specifications, model quality, materials and processes, occlusion and seating, and delivery deadlines into a deliverable and traceable restoration.

The work is mainly in a laboratory, mostly in a temperature-controlled indoor environment, requiring long periods of mostly seated fine manual work and equipment operation, with exposure to gypsum and metal dust, noise and some chemical materials; delivery deadlines are often set by clinical appointments, creating time pressure; units differ clearly (clinic-affiliated laboratories, commercial denture manufacturing enterprises, medical device manufacturing enterprises) in process division of labor, degree of digitalization, pay method and quality management system.

Similar adjacent job titles do not mean the same duties: distinguish the dentist's diagnosis, seating and clinical adjustment, the dental assistant's chairside assistance, the dental hygienist's examination and scaling, the optician's prescription eyewear dispensing, and the different processing objects of the ophthalmic laboratory technician and the medical appliance technician in the same group; whether one can discuss plans directly with the dentist and whether one can release finished products independently depends on the unit's quality management system and position authorization.

Inputs that must be verified: the work order and specifications (material, color, occlusion and contact requirements, seating time), impressions or intraoral scan data, model quality and disinfection requirements, denture materials and registration information, equipment parameters and process specifications. What must not be done: do not change specifications set by the dentist without authorization, do not use unregistered denture materials or materials of unknown origin, do not start work when models are damaged or scan data are unclear, and do not skip inspection and release finished products directly.

Fit judgments should combine laboratory mentoring observation, finished-product inspection records and dentist feedback, and are not replaced by an interest type or a single test; color vision, manual dexterity and spatial sense are ability requirements in real tasks that must be confirmed through actual operation and feedback.

All paper exercises on this page use fictitious materials; real patient impressions and scan data, model and finished-product disinfection, denture material use, and medical device production and product registration are carried out by qualified units and personnel under applicable regulations (such as mainland China's Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Medical Devices and the requirements for custom-made dentures, and the requirements of the applicable U.S. jurisdiction).

The work objects of dental laboratory technicians are the work orders and specifications issued by dentists or prosthodontists, the patient's oral impressions or intraoral scan data, and the restorations and appliances to be fabricated or repaired; the outputs are restorations meeting specifications (crowns, bridges, inlays, post-and-cores, removable and complete dentures, orthodontic appliances and so on), working models and digital exchange files, and traceable fabrication and inspection records; the basis for processing is prescription specifications and material instructions, dental prosthetics process requirements, denture material and production quality standards, and the unit's own process specifications, not the occupational title.

Check one: whether the work order and specifications are complete and clear — whether material and porcelain powder types, shade information, occlusion and contact requirements, and seating time are all stated; missing items must be queried with the dentist or handled through the clarification process specified by the unit, without guessing.

Check two: whether the impression, model and scan data allow work to start — check impression integrity, model distortion and damage, and the completeness and units of scan data; when they are inconsistent with the work order, return them for a new impression or mark them for verification according to the procedure.

Verify precision and occlusion on the model and articulator according to prescription specifications, with specific inspection items per the product's technical requirements; laboratory inspection and fitting on the model and articulator are separate from clinical try-in and adjustment on the patient; the 2026 guiding principles require seating and adjustment by a physician with professional qualifications, and technician experience or training or supervisor approval does not substitute for physician qualifications.

Check four: whether color and esthetics meet requirements — shade matching, porcelain build-up and glazing must be verified under the same light source and shade-matching conditions, and the porcelain powder used, layer thickness and sintering parameters recorded so that rework is reproducible.

Direction comparison first fixes the work object: whether it is the fabrication and repair of dental restorations and orthodontic appliances, or, within the same group, lens processing or brace and prosthesis fabrication, and then compares delivery rhythm, work environment and responsibility boundaries.

Direction one within the occupation leans toward traditional manual craft: modeling, wax patterns, investing and casting, porcelain build-up and polishing, suited to people who value hand feel, patience and repeated quality verification.

Direction two within the occupation leans toward digital design and processing: intraoral scan data processing, CAD design, CAM milling and additive manufacturing, requiring spatial modeling and parameter verification ability.

Direction three within the occupation leans toward quality and process management: process specifications, material and equipment management, inspection and traceability, mentoring and workstation coordination, requiring documentation and communication skills.
Direction one within the occupation: traditional manual craft (modeling, wax patterns, casting, porcelain build-up and polishing)

Model from the work order and impressions, make wax patterns and investment patterns, invest and cast, grind and polish, build up porcelain, sinter and shade match, and deliver hand-made crowns, bridges and dentures.

Compared with the digital direction, it relies more on hand feel, experience and repeated manual adjustment, takes longer per unit, and places high demands on color vision and hand stability; compared with adjacent occupations it does not involve chairside treatment, scaling or prescription eyewear dispensing.
If you prefer hand feel and fine craft and can accept repeated polishing and rework, you can start in the traditional craft direction.
Direction two within the occupation: digital design and processing (scanning, CAD, CAM and additive manufacturing)
Process intraoral and model scan data, design restorations with CAD software, drive milling or additive manufacturing equipment to produce the framework, and verify seating and occlusion parameters.

Compared with traditional craft, the processes are more standardized and can be collaborated on remotely, but one must master software and equipment parameters, data formats and precision verification; subsequent processes such as porcelain build-up, polishing and inspection are still required.
If you are interested in three-dimensional modeling, software operation and parameter verification, you can build up experience in the digital design and processing direction.
Direction three within the occupation: quality, process and production management

Compared with the other directions, the output shifts from single restorations to replicable processes and records, with responsibility covering the quality and traceability of an entire order batch, requiring documentation and communication skills.
If you are good at turning experience into written procedures and getting others to follow them, you can move toward quality and process management.
Adjacent occupations: dental assistants (31-9091.00) and dental hygienists (29-1292.00)

Dental assistants prepare and disinfect instruments, prepare patients, and assist and record during treatment under a dentist's direction; dental hygienists perform examinations, scaling and preventive procedures under their license; both work directly on patients' mouths, whereas this occupation processes restorations in the laboratory and usually does not provide clinical care directly; the transferable common points are infection control and instrument and model handling standards.
If you would rather interact with patients directly, compare these two directions; if you prefer independent processing and inspection, choose the laboratory direction.
Adjacent occupations: general dentists (29-1021.00) and medical assistants (31-9092.00)

General dentists are responsible for diagnosis, treatment plans, seating and clinical adjustment; medical assistants provide clinical and administrative support in general clinics; this occupation processes according to prescriptions and specifications, and the common points with the two are respectively communication related to restorations and patient reception and record handling.

If you want to make diagnostic and seating decisions, you need to follow the dental professional education and practice registration path; if you want to work in a general clinic, you can compare medical assistant.
Occupations in the same group: ophthalmic laboratory technicians (51-9083.00) and medical appliance technicians (51-9082.00)

All three belong to the official combined group 51-9080, but their objects differ: this occupation makes dental restorations, ophthalmic laboratory technicians cut, grind, polish and assemble lenses, and medical appliance technicians fabricate and fit braces, orthoses and prostheses; the wage and employment figures of the combined group cannot be taken as those of this subcategory alone.
If you are more interested in optical processing or the fabrication of orthoses and prostheses, you can compare within the same group before choosing a direction.

entries.answer: Read the requirements from the physician's work order and specifications, inspect models and impressions, fabricate and repair dentures, crowns, bridges, inlays, post-and-cores and orthodontic appliances, and verify seating, contact and occlusal precision with articulators, micrometers and model seating checks; this also includes grinding and polishing, porcelain build-up, sintering and shade matching, scanning models to generate digital files, repairing dentures and maintaining equipment; the final seating and clinical adjustment are performed by the dental physician.
entries.question: What does a dental laboratory technician do in a typical day?

entries.answer: The dental physician is responsible for diagnosis, seating and clinical adjustment; dental assistants assist chairside, handle instruments and keep records; dental hygienists perform oral examination, scaling and preventive procedures under their licence; this occupation processes restorations in the laboratory according to prescriptions and specifications, usually does not have direct patient contact, and cannot change prescription content or make clinical judgments on its own.
entries.question: How do dental laboratory technicians differ from dental assistants and dental hygienists?

entries.answer: This page gives no replacement conclusion. The official statement is that demand for dental technicians is expected to decline because of labour-saving technologies such as 3D printing, which is a directional judgment at the level of the occupation total; yet occlusion judgment, shade matching and esthetic finishing, rework decisions and clinical communication within this subcategory still rely on hand feel and experience. Whether replacement occurs and to what degree requires task-level evidence.
entries.question: How will AI affect or replace dental laboratory technicians?

entries.answer: What can be verified is the use of digital tools: intraoral and model scanning, CAD design software, and CAM milling and additive manufacturing equipment have long been used for data capture, shape design and framework processing; the official sources also list 3D printing as a technology affecting dental technician demand. These are evidence of technology and demand direction, not adoption-rate or job outcome data.
entries.question: For which tasks of dental laboratory technicians is there evidence of technology change?

entries.answer: Editorial suggestion: verify the work order, consistency of tooth position and material, software parameters, measured dimensions and inspection records; manual review and release follow the unit's quality system authorization, and NIST only provides an AI governance framework and does not regulate these specific dental processes.

description.text: Dental Laboratory Technicians (O*NET-SOC 51-9081.00) fabricate and repair dentures, crowns, bridges, inlays, post-and-cores and orthodontic appliances in the laboratory according to the dentist's prescription and specifications, using processes such as impressions and models, wax patterns, investing and casting, porcelain firing and sintering, resin build-up and grinding and polishing, and verify seating, contact and occlusal precision with articulators and measuring tools; they also process intraoral and model scan data, design with CAD and drive milling or additive manufacturing equipment, while recording material batches and process parameters for traceability; seating and clinical adjustment are the responsibility of the dental physician. The work context is an indoor environment requiring long periods of seated fine manual work and equipment operation, with exposure to dust, noise and some chemical materials. U.S. basis: in this occupation's May 2025 wage data the median annual wage is 49,610 USD (median hourly wage 23.85 USD) and the annual percentiles are 36,660／40,420／49,610／62,070／76,940 USD; about 34,400 people in 2025, a projected decline of about 6% in 2025—2035 (about 32,300 in 2035), and about 3,600 openings per year on average over the projection period including replacement needs; the U.S. official data combine this occupation with ophthalmic laboratory technicians (51-9083.00) and medical appliance technicians (51-9082.00) into group 51-9080 for statistics (combined group May 2025 median annual wage 47,060 USD, about 64,300 positions in 2025, a decline of about 2% in 2025—2035). Mainland China: the counterpart occupation is dental restoration fabricators (4-14-03-02); custom dentures are administered as Class II medical devices, and production must have the corresponding registration certificate and production licence; mainland China's published statistics do not release occupation-level wages corresponding to this occupation, and this page visibly marks the gap in the relevant places rather than filling it with an industry average.

subject.name: Dental Laboratory Technicians
subject.summary: Dental Laboratory Technicians (O*NET-SOC 51-9081.00) fabricate and repair dental restorations and appliances in the laboratory according to the dentist's or prosthodontist's prescription and specifications: reading the work order and specifications, inspecting impressions or intraoral scan data and models, making dies and occlusal records, and using processes such as wax patterns, investing and casting, porcelain firing and sintering, resin build-up and grinding and polishing to fabricate and repair dentures, crowns, bridges, inlays, post-and-cores and orthodontic appliances, while verifying seating, contact and occlusal precision with articulators and measuring tools; the outputs are deliverable restorations, working models and digital exchange files, and traceable fabrication and inspection records. Seating, clinical adjustment and the final diagnostic and treatment judgment are the responsibility of the dental physician. U.S. basis: O*NET-SOC 51-9081.00 is a single occupational code, and the BLS Occupational Outlook publishes both this subcategory and the 51-9080 combined group data formed by it together with ophthalmic laboratory technicians (51-9083.00) and medical appliance technicians (51-9082.00) in the same group, so the bases must be distinguished; in this occupation's May 2025 wage data the median annual wage is 49,610 USD (median hourly wage 23.85 USD), with about 34,400 people in 2025 and a projected decline of about 6% in 2025—2035. Mainland China basis: the counterpart occupation is dental restoration fabricators (occupational code 4-14-03-02); custom dentures are administered as Class II medical devices, and production requires a registration certificate and production licence together with compliance with good manufacturing practice; in this round the National Bureau of Statistics wage release consulted did not provide a figure listed separately for this occupation in mainland China, and this page retains the gap as it stands.
